\chapter{Hablamos --- the First Form That Is Not About One Person}
\label{ch:spanish-hablamos}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what we do, with the -amos ending.}

-mos is Latin's -mus, barely changed in two thousand years.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablamos]{hablamos — \textquotedblleft{}we speak\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-hablamos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}you speak\textquotedblright{} to a friend. (\emph{Hablo. Hablas.})
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the first form that is not about one person}]
Every verb form you have met so far — in every tense — has been about \textbf{one} person. That changes here.

Drop the \textbf{-ar}, add \textbf{-amos}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablamos} — \emph{we speak.}
\end{quote}

One word again, no pronoun, and now it covers you and somebody else.

This is the form you will reach for constantly and have not had: \emph{we speak}, \emph{we work}, \emph{we study}. Everything you could say about yourself, you can now say about a group you belong to.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{-mos} is remarkable for how little happened to it.

Latin marked \emph{we} with \textbf{-mus}: \emph{amāmus}, \textquotedblleft{}we love\textquotedblright{}. Spanish says \emph{-mos}. One vowel changed in two thousand years, and nothing else — no consonant lost, no syllable worn away, no analogy pulling it out of shape.

Compare what became of the third person, which lost its \textbf{-t} entirely (\emph{hablat} $\to$ \emph{habla}). Endings do not decay at the same rate, and this one barely decayed at all.

\textbf{And Portuguese and Italian kept it too} — \emph{falamos}, \emph{parliamo}. If you ever meet another Romance language, \emph{-mos} or \emph{-mo} will be waiting for you, doing the same job.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablamos\textquotedblright{} — one person, then a group
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablamos\textquotedblright{} alone, and notice it is still a whole sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}we speak\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Hablamos}.) Which Latin ending is that? (\textbf{-mus}, almost unchanged.) How many words? (\textbf{One} — still no pronoun.) Next: the form for \emph{them}.
\end{tcolorbox}
